messages.content:
You turn an incident review, written by a data-centre operator's own engineers after they solved a problem, into proposed changes to an "intelligence pill": a governed card of know-how that a facility team applies during the first hour of a cooling or power event.

You work only from the numbered sentences you are given. You add nothing from general knowledge.

Each change is one of:
- add_rule: a new piece of judgement. "when" = observable conditions a duty team could check; "then" = concrete actions; "why" = the reason the review gives; optional "escalate" = who must be called and on what trigger.
- amend_rule: add conditions or actions to an existing rule (give its rule_id) because this review sharpens it.
- add_guardrail: something the team or an assistant must not do or must not rely on.
- ask_expert: a question the review leaves open that an expert must answer before the pill can be trusted on it (for example a threshold, a time limit, who decides). Use this instead of guessing.

Hard rules:
1. Every add_rule, amend_rule and add_guardrail lists "evidence": the ids of the sentences that support it, copied exactly as they appear in review_sentences (for example "AZ-SCUS-2018:S9", with no prefix). No evidence, no change.
2. Never write a number (temperature, minutes, counts) that is not in a cited sentence. If a number matters but is missing, use ask_expert.
3. Write rules about facility operations (power, cooling, staffing, procedures, controls). Ignore cloud-software recovery details.
4. Prefer judgement over description: what an experienced engineer would check or do next, and why, not a retelling of the event.
5. If "focus_findings" are given, they are what the current pill failed to anticipate in this incident; make sure each one is either covered by a change or turned into ask_expert.

Reply with JSON only: {"changes": [ ... ]}. Shapes:
{"op":"add_rule","title":"...","when":["..."],"then":["..."],"why":"...","escalate":{"to":"...","trigger":"..."},"evidence":["<id copied from review_sentences>"]}
{"op":"amend_rule","rule_id":"R-001","add_when":["..."],"add_then":["..."],"why":"...","evidence":["<id copied from review_sentences>"]}
{"op":"add_guardrail","text":"...","evidence":["<id copied from review_sentences>"]}
{"op":"ask_expert","question":"...","why":"..."}

{"incident":{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019","title":"Cooling control system fails during a host failover; cooling shuts down instead of going to maximum (AWS Tokyo)","operator":"Amazon Web Services","site":"AP-NORTHEAST-1 (Tokyo), part of one Availability Zone"},"review_sentences":[{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S5","text":"The overheating was due to a control system failure that caused multiple, redundant cooling systems to fail in parts of the affected Availability Zone."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S18","text":"This event was caused by a failure of our datacenter control system, which is used to control and optimize the various cooling systems used in our datacenters."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S19","text":"The control system runs on multiple hosts for high availability."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S20","text":"This control system contains third-party code which allows it to communicate with third-party devices such as fans, chillers, and temperature sensors."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S21","text":"It communicates either directly or through embedded Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC) which in turn communicate with the actual devices."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S22","text":"Just prior to the event, the datacenter control system was in the process of failing away from one of the control hosts."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S23","text":"During this kind of failover, the control system has to exchange information with other control systems and the datacenter equipment it controls (e.g., the cooling equipment and temperature sensors throughout the datacenter) to ensure that the new control host has the most up-to-date information about the state of the datacenter."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S24","text":"Due to a bug in the third-party control system logic, this exchange resulted in excessive interactions between the control system and the devices in the datacenter which ultimately resulted in the control system becoming unresponsive."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S25","text":"Our datacenters are designed such that if the datacenter control system fails, the cooling systems go into maximum cooling mode until the control system functionality is restored."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S26","text":"While this worked correctly in most of the datacenter, in a small portion of the datacenter, the cooling system did not correctly transition to this safe cooling configuration and instead shut down."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S27","text":"As an added safeguard, our datacenter operators have the ability to bypass the datacenter control systems and put our cooling system in “purge” mode to quickly exhaust hot air in the event of a malfunction."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S28","text":"The team attempted to activate purge in the affected areas of the datacenter, but this also failed."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S29","text":"At this point, temperatures began to rise in the affected part of the datacenter and servers began to power off when they became too hot."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S30","text":"Because the datacenter control system was unavailable, the operations team had minimum visibility into the health and state of the datacenter cooling systems."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S31","text":"To recover, the team had to manually investigate and reset all of the affected pieces of equipment and put them into a maximum cooling configuration."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S32","text":"During this process, it was discovered that the PLCs controlling some of the air handling units were also unresponsive."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S33","text":"These controllers needed to be reset."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S34","text":"It was the failure of these PLC controllers which prevented the default cooling and “purge” mode from correctly working."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S35","text":"After these controllers were reset, cooling was restored to the affected area of the datacenter and temperatures began to decrease."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S36","text":"We are still working with our third-party vendors to understand the bug, and subsequent interactions, that caused both the control system and the impacted PLCs to become unresponsive."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S37","text":"In the interim, we have disabled the failover mode that triggered this bug on our control systems to ensure we do not have a recurrence of this issue."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S38","text":"We have also trained our local operations teams to quickly identify and remediate this situation if it were to recur, and we are confident that we could reset the system before seeing any customer impact if a similar situation was to occur for any reason."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S39","text":"Finally, we are working to modify the way that we control the impacted air handling units to ensure that “purge mode” is able to bypass the PLC controllers completely."},{"id":"AWS-NRT-2019:S40","text":"This is an approach we have begun using in our newest datacenter designs and will make us even more confident that “purge mode” will work even if PLCs become unresponsive."}],"current_pill":{"pill":"dc-cooling-loss@1.0.0","scope":{"assets":["data halls cooled by chilled-water plant (chillers, pumps, chilled-water loop)","utility and generator power feeding that plant"],"not_for":["IT service recovery and failover","fire suppression and life safety (follow the site emergency plan)"]},"rules":[{"id":"R-001","title":"Treat utility voltage swells as a cooling-plant threat, not just a power-transfer event","when":["storms are active in the area and the utility feed shows voltage sags or swells","a portion of the datacenter has transferred from utility power to generator power"],"then":["immediately verify that mechanical cooling systems are still running, rather than assuming surge suppressors protected them","if mechanical cooling has shut down, treat the datacenter as being on a load-dependent thermal buffer and start planning for its depletion","transfer the rest of the datacenter to generators to stabilize the power supply while storms are still active"],"why":"Voltage swells triggered a transfer to generator power and also shut down the mechanical cooling systems despite surge suppressors being in place; the site initially survived only on a load-dependent thermal buffer.","escalate":{"to":"facility operations lead and cooling plant engineer","trigger":"mechanical cooling confirmed shut down while storms remain active in the area"}},{"id":"R-002","title":"Act on thermal buffer depletion before automated shutdowns begin","when":["mechanical cooling is down and the datacenter is running on its load-dependent thermal buffer","datacenter temperature is approaching safe operational thresholds"],"then":["treat the thermal buffer as a finite resource and act before it is depleted","expect that once the buffer is gone, temperature will exceed safe operational thresholds and automated device shutdown will begin","recognize that in parts of the datacenter temperature can rise so quickly that hardware is damaged before it can shut down"],"why":"Once the thermal buffer was depleted the datacenter exceeded safe operational thresholds and automated shutdown began, but temperatures rose so quickly in places that some hardware was damaged before it could shut down.","escalate":{"to":"incident commander","trigger":"thermal buffer depletion is imminent or automated shutdowns have started"}}],"guardrails":[{"id":"G-001","text":"Do not rely on surge suppressors alone to keep mechanical cooling available during utility voltage swells; the review records that cooling shut down despite surge suppressors being in place."},{"id":"G-002","text":"Do not assume onsite redundancies make customer workloads safe from a datacenter cooling failure; the review states there are scenarios in which a cooling failure can impact customer workloads in the affected datacenter."}]},"focus_findings":[{"id":"F1","kind":"root_cause","text":"Due to a bug in the third-party control system logic, this exchange resulted in excessive interactions between the control system and the devices in the datacenter which ultimately resulted in the control system becoming unresponsive."},{"id":"F3","kind":"contributing_factor","text":"It was the failure of these PLC controllers which prevented the default cooling and “purge” mode from correctly working."},{"id":"F4","kind":"contributing_factor","text":"Because the datacenter control system was unavailable, the operations team had minimum visibility into the health and state of the datacenter cooling systems."},{"id":"F5","kind":"response","text":"To recover, the team had to manually investigate and reset all of the affected pieces of equipment and put them into a maximum cooling configuration."},{"id":"F6","kind":"remediation","text":"In the interim, we have disabled the failover mode that triggered this bug on our control systems to ensure we do not have a recurrence of this issue."},{"id":"F7","kind":"remediation","text":"We have also trained our local operations teams to quickly identify and remediate this situation if it were to recur, and we are confident that we could reset the system before seeing any customer impact if a similar situation was to occur for any reason."},{"id":"F8","kind":"remediation","text":"Finally, we are working to modify the way that we control the impacted air handling units to ensure that “purge mode” is able to bypass the PLC controllers completely."},{"id":"F9","kind":"impact","text":"It took longer to recover these instances and volumes and some needed to be retired as a result of failures to the underlying hardware."}]}
